note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Understand how learning works in a discipline's discourse community

evidence.title: Map of your discipline as a community of practice
evidence.example: You map your discipline as a community using Lave and Wenger's (1991) idea of legitimate peripheral participation: newcomers learn by taking part in real but limited ways and move towards full participation. You mark where you are now as a newcomer and the activities, such as seminars, reading and writing, that move you inward. This shows you understand how learning works in your discipline's discourse community (for example, a first-year archaeology student placing themselves relative to lecturers who excavate and publish).
evidence.artefact: A labelled diagram of your discipline's community showing your position and the activities that move you towards fuller participation.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

evidence.title: Notes from a research seminar on how the discipline argues
evidence.example: You attend a real event in your discipline's community, such as a departmental research seminar, a guest lecture or a learned society meeting, and note how people talk, argue and use evidence there. You then write a short account of what this taught you about how the discipline learns. This shows you understanding a discourse community from the inside (for example, a physics student noting how a speaker's results were questioned at a colloquium).
evidence.artefact: Event notes and a short account of the community's ways of talking, arguing and using evidence.
grounding: professional: Learns how a profession or organisation works, its norms, people and ways of knowing, on joining it.

genericOutcomes.title: Core knowledge traced to a community's shared practice
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how a discipline's core knowledge is established and legitimised through participation in its community of practice, rather than through isolated facts.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a core topic in a field and trace how its accepted knowledge came to be accepted: who established it, what evidence convinced the community, and how newcomers are taught to use it. Using the idea of legitimate peripheral participation, you show that broad, well-founded knowledge of the subject's content grows through taking part in the community that produces and tests it, not from isolated facts alone.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short trace of one core topic showing how community practice established and tested the knowledge.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

genericOutcomes.title: Core knowledge checked against a community of practitioners
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can check their understanding of a core topic against how practitioners in the discipline actually apply and test it.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a core idea you hold in a field and check it against how practitioners in that field actually use and test it, by asking a knowledgeable contact, reading a professional source or observing real practice, to see whether your understanding matches theirs. You note where your grasp was accurate and where it needed adjusting. This demonstrates broad and well-founded knowledge built through engagement with the field's working community.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note comparing your understanding of a core idea with how practitioners in the field use it.
grounding: professional: Learns how a profession or organisation works, its norms, people and ways of knowing, on joining it.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

capabilities.statement: Tell formative from summative assessment and engage with varied forms

evidence.title: Module assessments sorted and aligned to outcomes
evidence.example: You list the assessments in one module, label each formative or summative, and use Biggs' (1996) constructive alignment to show which learning outcome each is designed to check. You then note how you will use the formative tasks to prepare for the summative ones. This shows you can tell the two apart and engage with varied forms (for example, a first-year marketing student seeing that a practice pitch prepares for the assessed group presentation).
evidence.artefact: A module assessment table labelled formative or summative, each linked to an outcome, with your plan for using the formative tasks.
grounding: ing:doc:constructive-alignment-biggs-1996

evidence.title: Optional formative draft used to improve a marked piece
evidence.example: You take part in a formative task you could skip, such as a draft submission, a practice quiz or a peer review, and use the feedback to change the final piece before it is marked. This shows you engaging with varied assessment forms and treating rehearsal as a chance to improve (for example, a film studies student submitting an essay plan for comment and restructuring the argument as a result).
evidence.artefact: Your formative draft with its feedback, beside the summative submission showing the changes you made.
grounding: professional: Uses practice runs, drafts and reviews as chances to improve before work is judged.

genericOutcomes.title: Formative and summative purposes distinguished by function
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can distinguish formative from summative assessment by purpose, timing and the role each plays in improving or recording performance.
genericOutcomes.example: You take two pieces of assessment, one intended to improve your work in progress and one intended to record a final result, and set out how each one's purpose, timing and use of feedback differs, using constructive alignment to show how the formative piece feeds into the summative one. This demonstrates differentiating formative from summative assessment and engaging with the varied forms each purpose produces.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short comparison of two assessments setting out their differing purpose, timing and use of feedback.
grounding: ing:doc:constructive-alignment-biggs-1996
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Varied forms of judgement engaged with on their own terms
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can engage appropriately with different forms of assessment, adjusting their approach according to whether a form is meant to improve or to record their work.
genericOutcomes.example: Across a period of work, you take part in several different forms through which your work is judged, some formal and recorded, some informal and intended only to help you improve, and you adjust how seriously you treat each one to match its actual purpose. You record which form helped you improve most and why. This demonstrates differentiating formative from summative judgement and engaging with varied assessment forms.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of different forms of judgement encountered, each labelled by purpose, with the most useful one identified.
grounding: professional: Uses practice runs, drafts and reviews as chances to improve before work is judged.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Tell active, constructivist learning from passive reception

evidence.title: Two study sessions compared as deep and surface approaches
evidence.example: You record two study sessions on the same reading, one spent rereading and highlighting and one spent questioning, summarising in your own words and linking to earlier topics. Using Marton and Saljo's (1976) distinction between deep and surface approaches, you explain which session was active and constructivist and what you could explain afterwards. This shows you can tell active learning from passive reception (for example, a philosophy student comparing their grasp of a Kant extract after each session).
evidence.artefact: Notes from both sessions side by side, with a short commentary classifying each approach and what you could explain afterwards.
grounding: ing:doc:approaches-to-learning-marton-saljo-1976

evidence.title: Learning a work task actively instead of waiting to be shown
evidence.example: In a job, volunteering or society role, you notice a point where you were waiting to be told what to do and instead learn it actively: asking questions, trying it and checking your understanding. You write up the contrast. This shows you distinguishing active from passive learning in practice (for example, a computing student in a summer IT support job learning a ticketing system by working through real requests rather than reading the manual).
evidence.artefact: A short before-and-after account of learning a task at work, confirmed by a note from your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Takes an active part in own learning at work rather than waiting to be trained.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

genericOutcomes.title: Core content tested through a deep approach to study
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how a deep, questioning approach to study produces more well-founded subject knowledge than passive, surface-level reading.
genericOutcomes.example: You pick one piece of core subject content and study it twice, once by simply reading it and once by questioning it, relating it to what you already know and testing whether you can explain it unprompted. Drawing on the distinction between deep and surface approaches to learning, you show that broad, well-founded knowledge comes from the deep approach, and you set out the evidence of understanding each one produced.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short comparison of what you could explain after a surface reading versus a deep, questioning study.
grounding: ing:doc:approaches-to-learning-marton-saljo-1976
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

genericOutcomes.title: Well-founded knowledge built by active questioning on the job
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can build well-founded knowledge by actively questioning procedures and explanations rather than accepting them at face value.
genericOutcomes.example: Rather than accepting a procedure or explanation at face value, you actively question it, asking why it works, testing it against a case you know, and checking your revised understanding with someone experienced. You record what changed in your grasp of the underlying knowledge as a result. This demonstrates broad and well-founded knowledge built through an active rather than a passive approach to learning.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of a procedure questioned, tested and checked, with what your understanding changed to.
grounding: professional: Takes an active part in own learning at work rather than waiting to be trained.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

capabilities.statement: Interpret learning outcomes and how activities align to them

evidence.title: Alignment grid tracing outcomes to activities and assessment
evidence.example: You take the intended learning outcomes for a module, pick out the verb in each, and trace how lectures, seminars and the assessment are aligned to them, using Biggs' (1996) constructive alignment. Where an outcome has no clear matching activity, you note how you will practise it yourself. This shows you interpreting outcomes and how activities align to them (for example, a civil engineering student linking 'design a beam' to tutorial calculations and the design project).
evidence.artefact: An alignment grid: each outcome, its verb, the matching activities and assessment, and your own actions for any gaps.
grounding: ing:doc:constructive-alignment-biggs-1996

evidence.title: Everyday tasks mapped to role objectives with a supervisor
evidence.example: In a job, placement or society role, you take the objectives or performance standards you are given, work out how your everyday tasks contribute to each, and discuss the mapping with your supervisor. This shows you reading objectives and seeing how tasks relate to them, as you do with learning outcomes (for example, a hospitality management student mapping hotel reception duties to the guest satisfaction targets in their appraisal).
evidence.artefact: A mapping of your tasks to your role objectives, annotated after discussion with your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Reads objectives and performance standards and sees how tasks and appraisal relate to them.

genericOutcomes.title: Assessment criteria traced back to stated outcomes
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse how assessment criteria, activities and stated learning outcomes are aligned, identifying any mismatch between them.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a set of assessment criteria and trace each one back to the specific learning outcome it is meant to measure, using constructive alignment to check that the criteria, the outcome and the activities that prepare for it all point the same way. Where the link is unclear, you note the mismatch. This demonstrates interpreting how assessment criteria are articulated and related to stated learning outcomes.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short trace linking each assessment criterion to its learning outcome, with any mismatches noted.
grounding: ing:doc:constructive-alignment-biggs-1996
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.31

genericOutcomes.title: Review criteria matched to agreed goals before work begins
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate, before starting a task, whether the criteria it will be judged against clearly relate to its intended outcomes.
genericOutcomes.example: Before starting a piece of work that will be judged, you check that the criteria it will be judged against are clearly related to the goals you have been set, and raise it if a criterion does not obviously connect to a stated goal. You keep a short note of the check and any clarification you sought. This demonstrates interpreting how judging criteria relate to intended outcomes.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note checking judging criteria against stated goals, with any clarification sought and received.
grounding: professional: Reads objectives and performance standards and sees how tasks and appraisal relate to them.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.31

capabilities.statement: Turn feedback into an action plan through reflection

evidence.title: Feedback turned into an action plan by reflection-on-action
evidence.example: You take feedback on a marked assignment and use Schon's (1983) reflection-on-action to look back at the decisions you made while writing it, asking why you made them and what the feedback suggests instead. You turn this into an action plan with specific, dated changes for the next assignment. This shows you using reflective practice to turn feedback into improvement (for example, a social work student reviewing comments on how they applied legislation in a case study).
evidence.artefact: Annotated feedback, a reflection on your decisions and an action plan of specific, dated changes.
grounding: ing:doc:reflective-practitioner-schon-1983

evidence.title: Supervisor feedback acted on through a short development plan
evidence.example: You turn appraisal or supervisor feedback from a job, placement or volunteering role into a short development plan, act on it over several weeks and review the outcome with the person who gave the feedback. This shows you using feedback to plan improvement beyond the classroom (for example, a retail management student acting on a shift manager's comments about handling customer complaints).
evidence.artefact: Feedback notes, your development plan and a follow-up review signed or emailed by your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Acts on appraisal and colleague feedback through a development plan.
professional: Vitae RDF B3: professional and career development

genericOutcomes.title: Reflection used to turn comment into a dated action plan
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse feedback through deliberate reflection to identify why a gap occurred and convert that analysis into a dated action plan.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a piece of feedback and, instead of reacting to it immediately, pause to reflect on the thinking that led to the original decision, why the feedback differs from it, and what a better decision would look like. You then convert that reflection into an action plan with specific, dated steps. This demonstrates turning feedback into an action plan through deliberate reflection rather than quick, unexamined response.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflection on one piece of feedback, with an action plan of specific, dated steps that followed.
grounding: ing:doc:reflective-practitioner-schon-1983
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Feedback converted into a tracked plan for improvement
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can convert feedback received on their work into a tracked plan of dated actions and review progress against it over time.
genericOutcomes.example: After receiving feedback on something you produced, you set aside time to reflect on it properly rather than responding at once, identify what it means for how you work, and write a short plan of dated actions. You check back against the plan after a set period to see what changed. This demonstrates converting feedback into a tracked plan for improvement through structured reflection.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated action plan drawn from one piece of feedback, with a later check against what changed.
grounding: professional: Acts on appraisal and colleague feedback through a development plan.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Apply self-regulated learning cycles to independent study

evidence.title: Two documented cycles of self-regulated independent study
evidence.example: You plan, monitor and review a block of independent study using Zimmerman's (2002) cyclical model of self-regulated learning: forethought (setting goals and strategies), performance (monitoring as you work) and self-reflection (evaluating results). You complete at least two full cycles and show how the second changed in light of the first. This shows you applying self-regulated learning to independent study (for example, a modern languages student preparing for an oral exam through weekly practice cycles).
evidence.artefact: Two completed cycle records, covering forethought, performance and self-reflection, showing what changed between the first and second.
grounding: model: Cyclical model of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002)

evidence.title: Progress log kept across a live client brief
evidence.example: During a long independent project, such as a dissertation, a self-directed lab project or a live client brief, you set weekly goals, keep a progress log and adjust your approach at set review points, sharing the log with your supervisor. This shows you applying self-regulated cycles to real independent work (for example, a product design student running a twelve-week brief for a local charity).
evidence.artefact: A project progress log with weekly goals, monitoring notes and recorded adjustments, shared with your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Plans own work and development, monitors progress against goals and adjusts approach.
professional: Vitae RDF B2: self-management

genericOutcomes.title: Independent study managed through a full regulation cycle
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how setting goals, monitoring progress and evaluating outcomes form a self-regulated cycle that sustains independent study.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a period of independent study and show how you manage it without direction from anyone else, by running it through a full cycle: setting your own goals and strategies, monitoring your progress as you go, and evaluating what worked once you have finished. You identify one adjustment the cycle produced. This demonstrates managing your own learning and working independently through a self-regulated cycle rather than by chance.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short account of one independent study cycle, its goals, monitoring and the adjustment it produced.
grounding: model: Cyclical model of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

genericOutcomes.title: Self-directed work regulated without outside direction
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can manage a piece of independent work by setting their own targets, tracking progress against them and adjusting their approach without external direction.
genericOutcomes.example: You take on a piece of work with no set schedule of check-ins, and manage it yourself, setting your own targets, tracking progress against them at intervals you choose, and changing your plan when progress falls short. You keep a brief log others could use to see how you managed the work independently. This demonstrates managing your own learning and working independently through a deliberate, self-regulated cycle.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A brief self-management log showing targets set, progress tracked and changes made without outside direction.
grounding: professional: Plans own work and development, monitors progress against goals and adjusts approach.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/independent-and-self-directed-learning

capabilities.statement: Adapt to the demands of different types of assessment

evidence.title: Three assessment types compared by the thinking they demand
evidence.example: Across three assessment types, such as an exam, a reflective portfolio and a group report, you analyse the command verbs and criteria with Bloom's revised taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001) to identify the level of thinking each demands, and adapt your preparation and writing to match. This shows you adapting to the demands of different types of assessment (for example, a politics student seeing that a policy brief asks them to evaluate and recommend, while an exam answer asks them to explain).
evidence.artefact: A comparison sheet for three assessments: verbs, Bloom's levels, and how you adapted your approach for each.
grounding: model: Revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001)

evidence.title: Briefing written for a real external audience
evidence.example: You produce work for a real audience in a form judged outside the university, such as a pitch to a business, a report for a community group or a funding bid for a society, and adapt your approach to that form's expectations. You note what differed from academic genres. This shows you adapting to the forms in which work is judged (for example, an environmental science student writing a two-page flood-risk briefing for a parish council).
evidence.artefact: The finished piece for the external audience, their response, and a short note on how you adapted to the form.
grounding: professional: Adapts to the forms in which work is judged: reports, pitches, reviews and audits.

genericOutcomes.title: Criteria compared across assessment types for consistency
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique how published criteria for different assessment types encode different levels of cognitive demand, despite assessing related learning outcomes.
genericOutcomes.example: You take the published criteria for two different types of assessment and compare how each criterion is articulated and related to the stated learning outcomes, noting where the demands differ even though both are checking related knowledge. Using a revised taxonomy of thinking skills, you identify the different level of thinking each form of assessment requires. This demonstrates adapting to differing demands while recognising the shared outcomes behind them.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A comparison of criteria across two assessment types, showing the differing demands and their shared outcomes.
grounding: model: Revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl 2001)
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.31

genericOutcomes.title: Preparation adapted once criteria for a form are read
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify and adapt their approach to preparing for a given form of assessment based on a careful reading of its specific criteria.
genericOutcomes.example: Before producing a piece of work, you read how the judging criteria are articulated for that particular form and check how they relate to the outcome you are meant to be meeting, then adjust your preparation accordingly rather than using your usual method regardless of form. You note one way your approach changed as a result. This demonstrates adapting to the demands of different types of assessment.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note on judging criteria read beforehand and the resulting change to your preparation.
grounding: professional: Adapts to the forms in which work is judged: reports, pitches, reviews and audits.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.31

capabilities.statement: Assess own and peers' work against marking criteria

evidence.title: Exemplar and own draft marked using Sadler's conditions
evidence.example: You mark an exemplar and then your own draft against the published marking criteria, using Sadler's (1989) conditions for improvement: knowing the standard, comparing your work with it and acting to close the gap. You justify each judgement with evidence from the text and compare your marks with a tutor's. This shows you assessing work against criteria (for example, a biomedical science student marking a lab report exemplar before self-assessing their own report).
evidence.artefact: A marked exemplar and self-assessed draft with criterion-by-criterion justifications, plus a comparison with the tutor's mark.
grounding: model: Conditions for closing the gap through feedback (Sadler 1989)

evidence.title: Criterion-based peer review in a team code review
evidence.example: You act as a reviewer in a real process, such as structured peer review on your module, editing for a society publication or a team code review, giving criterion-based comments on others' work before submission and receiving them on your own. This shows you reviewing work against agreed standards, as colleagues do before work is released (for example, a software engineering student reviewing teammates' pull requests against the team's coding standards).
evidence.artefact: Your written review comments mapped to the criteria, and the responses or changes they led to.
grounding: professional: Reviews own and colleagues' work against agreed standards before it is submitted or published.
professional: Carless and Boud (2018): making judgements

genericOutcomes.title: Own work judged against clearly articulated criteria
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify a mark for a piece of work by evaluating it criterion by criterion against clearly articulated standards.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a finished piece of your own work and a published set of criteria, and judge the work against each criterion in turn, writing a short justification for the mark you would give. You then compare your judgement with an expert mark to see where your reading of the criteria matched or differed. This demonstrates assessing work against criteria that are clearly articulated and related to stated standards.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A self-assessment against a published set of criteria, with justifications and a comparison to an expert mark.
grounding: model: Conditions for closing the gap through feedback (Sadler 1989)
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.31

genericOutcomes.title: Peer work judged against shared, explicit standards
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique a peer's work against shared, explicit standards and give criterion-by-criterion feedback rather than a general impression.
genericOutcomes.example: You review a colleague's work against a shared, explicit set of standards, writing comments tied to each one rather than a general impression, and you ask for the same kind of review on your own work in return. You note any criterion where you and your reviewer read the standard differently. This demonstrates assessing work against clearly articulated criteria that are applied consistently by more than one reviewer.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Criterion-by-criterion review comments exchanged with a colleague, with any disagreement in reading the standard noted.
grounding: professional: Reviews own and colleagues' work against agreed standards before it is submitted or published.
benchmark: qaa/psychology-2023/3.31

capabilities.statement: Use feedback in dialogue with tutors to sustain development across a degree

evidence.title: Cross-module feedback analysis using four features of feedback literacy
evidence.example: You review the feedback you have received across your degree and analyse it with Carless and Boud's (2018) four features of feedback literacy: appreciating feedback, making judgements, managing affect and taking action. You identify recurring themes, show how you acted on them, and set out how you will keep using feedback beyond the course. This shows you using feedback diagnostically to sustain development (for example, a master's student in education tracing a recurring comment about critical synthesis).
evidence.artefact: A cross-module feedback analysis with recurring themes, evidence of action taken and a plan linked to the four features.
grounding: ing:doc:feedback-literacy-carless-boud-2018

evidence.title: Feedback meetings you prepare for and lead across a term
evidence.example: You arrange and lead feedback conversations with a tutor, supervisor or manager over a term, bringing your own questions and a summary of what you have changed since the last meeting, and you record what you agree. This shows you seeking feedback actively and using dialogue to build on it over time (for example, a postgraduate translation student meeting a dissertation supervisor fortnightly with a list of queries on drafts).
evidence.artefact: Meeting records across a term showing your questions, the actions agreed and the changes made between meetings.
grounding: professional: Seeks feedback actively, discusses it with managers and colleagues and builds on it over time.
professional: Carless and Boud (2018): appreciating feedback, taking action

genericOutcomes.title: Recurring feedback used to deepen core knowledge over time
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can synthesise feedback received over an extended period to diagnose a recurring theme and explain how resolving it deepens their core subject knowledge.
genericOutcomes.example: You trace one theme that keeps recurring in feedback on your work over an extended period, and use the four features of feedback literacy, appreciating, judging, managing affect and acting, to work out why the same issue keeps appearing and what change would finally resolve it. You show how addressing it has deepened your broad, well-founded grasp of the subject's core content. This demonstrates using feedback diagnostically to sustain development.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A trace of one recurring feedback theme, the four-feature analysis applied to it and the resulting change in understanding.
grounding: ing:doc:feedback-literacy-carless-boud-2018
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

genericOutcomes.title: Dialogue with a reviewer used to build core knowledge
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can sustain an ongoing dialogue with a reviewer across several rounds of feedback, agreeing actions that build their grasp of core material over time.
genericOutcomes.example: Rather than treating each round of feedback as separate, you deliberately raise it in conversation with the person reviewing your work, asking how it connects to comments from earlier rounds, and agree specific actions before the next piece of work. Over several rounds you track how your grasp of the core material has broadened as a result. This demonstrates sustaining development through active dialogue rather than one-off responses to feedback.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record across several feedback rounds showing the dialogue, agreed actions and the resulting growth in understanding.
grounding: professional: Seeks feedback actively, discusses it with managers and colleagues and builds on it over time.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding
